1.pericope_label: The word of the Lord came again unto me, saying, Son of man, set thy face against the Ammonites, and prophesy against them
debates: Why the prophet turns from Israel to the nations
What setting the face against them means
How the message reached a people the prophet was far from
outliers: Gill supposes the word delivered through Ammonite ambassadors or merchants at Babylon or by letters, while Henry stresses that the prophet knew little of those nations and spoke by the spirit of prophecy as if he had been among them
Keil and Delitzsch find a symbolical significance in the number seven, both in the count of nations and in the seven separate words directed against Egypt
themes: A prophet setting his face as a flint
A besieger casting lots between two capitals
Neighbours who should have pitied and instead cheered
A captive told what nations he cannot see are doing

4.pericope_label: Behold, therefore I will deliver thee to the men of the east for a possession, and they shall set their palaces in thee, and make their dwellings in thee
debates: Who the men of the east are
Whether knowing the Lord here means conversion or only defeat
outliers: Ellicott insists the closing formula means no penitent recognition of the Lord but only an experience of his wrath too plain to deny, where Wesley reads it as strangers brought into acquaintance with God and calls it a blessed effect of their calamities
Ellicott alone distinguishes the men of the east as possessors rather than conquerors, the conquest itself having been made by Nebuchadnezzar
themes: Palaces that are really folds for cattle
A royal city turned into a camel stable
Ruins of a later city on the site of a vanished one
A name that survives only in history books

8.pericope_label: Thus saith the Lord God; Because that Moab and Seir do say, Behold, the house of Judah is like unto all the heathen
debates: What the taunt about being like the heathen means
Why Seir is named beside Moab
Whose the frontier cities of Moab were
outliers: Ellicott holds that the division between the verses seriously obscures the sense, since the men of the east are given both nations at once rather than Moab alone

Clarke grounds the charge in a broken league with Zedekiah and a suspected defection to the Chaldeans, where Keil and Delitzsch make the sin a despising of the divine election of Israel and Henry a double triumph over its apostasies and its calamities
themes: A neighbour pleased to watch a religion decay
A shoulder opened to let an enemy in
Frontier towns that had changed hands four times
A land the Arabs still call the best there is

12.pericope_label: Thus saith the Lord God; Because that Edom hath dealt against the house of Judah by taking vengeance, and hath greatly offended, and revenged himself upon them
debates: Why Edom is charged more heavily than Ammon and Moab
Whether the prophecy points beyond vengeance to conversion
outliers: Clarke calls Teman and Dedan cities of the Moabites, where Ellicott makes Teman a southern district of Edom and Wesley a country on its southern coast

Ellicott rejects the reading, held by many commentators, that the prophecy intimates the ultimate conversion of Edom and its incorporation into the Church, as foreign both to the series and to the immediate connection
themes: An elder brother who never accepted the younger precedence
Enemies waylaying fugitives from a fallen city
A threat that spans a country from end to end
A conquered nation absorbed until its name vanishes

15.pericope_label: Thus saith the Lord God; Because the Philistines have dealt by revenge, and have taken vengeance with a despiteful heart, to destroy it for the old hatred
debates: Why the Philistines fall under the same sentence
outliers: Wesley makes the Cherethim the bowmen, the strength of Philistia, where Ellicott takes them for a coastal portion of the people whose name many equate with Cretans, an etymology he calls doubtful

Clarke gives an immediate occasion, that they had helped the Tyrians during the siege, while Ellicott accounts for their disappearance by the position of their land on the highway between contending empires
themes: A people combining two other nations sins
A phrase that reads as slaying the slayers
A coast road between two great powers
A remnant left over from four earlier swords
